## The freedom to choose what?

Imagine a town built around one large employer.

The company provides jobs. The workers provide labor. Together, they produce something valuable. There are gains from cooperation. But there is also conflict: the company may want lower costs, higher output, and fewer constraints; workers may want higher wages, safer conditions, and cleaner air. The question is not whether people are "free" in the abstract. The question is what choices they actually have.

If the company can leave but the workers cannot, one kind of bargain is possible. If workers have good outside options, organize politically, or change the law, a different bargain becomes possible. The [**rules of the game**]{.term data-example="Rules about work hours, pollution, unionization, contracts, and property determine what Bunker Hill and its workers can do, and who captures the gains from cooperation."} shape who can act, who must adjust, and who receives the benefits of progress.

Hayek asks a related question from another angle. Even if a society wants prosperity, how can it possibly know what to produce, where resources should go, and which plans are worth pursuing? His answer is prices. Prices communicate dispersed knowledge that no planner can gather in one place.

**The question this session is about: when do liberty, property rights, innovation, and progress reinforce each other, and when do the rules of the game make "liberty" unequally shared?**

::: {.instructor}
This is the "markets need institutions, and institutions allocate power" session. Use Hayek to explain why decentralized decision-making matters. Use UOE Chapters 1 and 2 to show that the ability to act on knowledge depends on rules, outside options, bargaining power, and democratic change.
:::

## Prices as compressed knowledge

Hayek's central claim is simple and radical: the knowledge needed to coordinate an economy is dispersed among millions of people.

A farmer knows local soil and weather. A machinist knows which tool is wearing out. A parent knows the timing constraints of a child's school day. A shop owner knows which goods are not moving. A scientist knows which experiment failed last week. None of this knowledge can be fully written down, sent to a ministry, and optimized from the center.

Prices help solve this problem. A price is not merely a number. It is a signal that compresses information about scarcity, opportunity, cost, demand, and alternative uses. When the price of copper rises, millions of people do not need to know exactly which mine flooded or which technology increased demand. They only need to know that copper has become more valuable at the margin, and they can adjust.

> Prices allow people to coordinate using knowledge they do not personally possess.

This is why Hayek thinks [**markets**]{.term data-example="A higher copper price tells buyers and sellers to economize or expand supply without requiring everyone to know the full story behind the shortage."} are epistemic institutions, not just incentive machines. They help societies use knowledge that exists only in fragments.

::: {.discuss}
Hayek says prices communicate knowledge. What kinds of knowledge do prices communicate poorly or not at all? Think about pollution, care work, public health, or scientific research.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="quiz">
  <p class="quiz-q">What is Hayek's main argument in "The Use of Knowledge in Society"?</p>
  <ol class="quiz-opts">
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Hayek's argument is almost the opposite: no central authority can possess all the relevant local knowledge.">A central planner can coordinate an economy if it has enough data.</li>
    <li data-correct="true" data-fb="Correct. Prices communicate dispersed knowledge and help people coordinate without requiring anyone to know the whole system.">Prices help coordinate dispersed knowledge that no single person or agency can collect.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Hayek is not arguing that all knowledge is scientific. Much of the relevant knowledge is local, tacit, and practical.">Only scientific experts have economically useful knowledge.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Hayek thinks politics and planning often distort the price system, but his argument is about knowledge and coordination, not simply selfishness.">Markets work because people ignore information from others.</li>
  </ol>
</div>
```

::: {.instructor}
Board move: draw two columns, "knowledge in one place" and "knowledge dispersed." Ask students what kind of knowledge a central planner could know, and what kind would be lost. Then ask where prices help and where they fail.
:::

## Rules and Permission to Act

Prices can only coordinate action if people are allowed to act on them.

That is why property rights matter. If you cannot own land securely, you will not invest in improving it. If contracts are not enforced, trade becomes risky. If officials can seize profits, entrepreneurs hide rather than expand. If entry into a profession or market depends on political connections, talent is wasted.

But property rights are not magic words. They are political arrangements. Someone decides whose property counts, whose contracts are enforced, whose harms are ignored, and who has standing to challenge abuse. A society can have property rights for some people and insecurity for others. It can have markets that work well for insiders and badly for outsiders.

UOE makes this point by treating institutions as rules of the game. The rules determine who moves first, what each person can do, what happens if a bargain fails, and whether a third party such as the government can change the feasible set.

> Liberty matters for progress when many people have real permission to use their knowledge, invest in the future, and challenge rules that exclude them.

::: {.discuss}
Can a society have secure property rights and still have unfair or inefficient rules? Whose rights would be secure, and whose choices would remain constrained?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="quiz">
  <p class="quiz-q">Why are property rights important for progress?</p>
  <ol class="quiz-opts">
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Property rights do not eliminate risk; they shape which risks people are willing to take.">They remove all uncertainty from economic life.</li>
    <li data-correct="true" data-fb="Correct. Secure rights make investment, exchange, and experimentation more attractive because people expect to keep enough of the returns.">They give people confidence to invest, trade, and experiment because the returns are more secure.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="This is too narrow. Property rights can support markets, but they are defined and enforced politically.">They make politics irrelevant to markets.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Strong property rights for a narrow elite can coexist with exclusion and extraction.">They guarantee that everyone benefits equally from growth.</li>
  </ol>
</div>
```

::: {.instructor}
The likely student mistake is to treat "property rights" as morally self-evident rather than institutionally designed. Ask: property rights for whom, over what, enforced by whom, against whom? This is where UOE complicates a simple Hayekian frame.
:::

## Outside Options and Power

Voluntary exchange is not automatically equal exchange.

In UOE, an [**outside option**]{.term data-example="A worker's outside option is what they can get if they do not work for the firm; a firm's outside option is what it can get if it closes, relocates, or invests elsewhere."} is what a person or organization can get if a particular interaction breaks down. Outside options matter because they set the threat point in a bargain. If a worker can easily find another good job, the firm must offer more. If the worker has nowhere else to go, the firm can capture more of the gains from cooperation.

This gives us a more precise way to talk about power. Power is not only coercion. It can be built into the structure of choices: who has alternatives, who moves first, who can wait, who can organize, who can appeal to the law, and who bears the cost of failure.

> Power shapes progress by determining who can refuse a bad bargain and who can change the rules that govern bargaining.

::: {.discuss}
Give an example of a market interaction where both sides choose voluntarily, but one side has much more power. What outside options make that possible?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="quiz">
  <p class="quiz-q">In UOE, why do outside options matter for liberty and progress?</p>
  <ol class="quiz-opts">
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Outside options are not only psychological. They describe what people can actually get if an interaction fails.">They measure how optimistic people feel about the future.</li>
    <li data-correct="true" data-fb="Correct. Outside options shape what people can demand, what they must accept, and how gains from cooperation are divided.">They determine what each side can get if a bargain breaks down, which shapes bargaining power.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Outside options are about alternatives, not about eliminating all conflict.">They make conflicts of interest disappear.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Prices remain important in Hayek's account. UOE adds a bargaining and institutional layer.">They replace prices as the only information in the economy.</li>
  </ol>
</div>
```

::: {.instructor}
Good board exercise: put two parties on the board, then change one outside option at a time. Ask students what happens to the feasible bargain and to each party's share of the gains from cooperation.
:::

## Changing the Rules

Progress threatens existing arrangements.

New technologies threaten old firms. New rules threaten old privileges. New forms of political participation threaten old settlements. But the rules can also be changed to make progress broader: limiting pollution, changing work hours, expanding education, enforcing contracts more fairly, or strengthening competition.

This is where Hayek and UOE fit together. Hayek explains why decentralized knowledge matters. UOE explains why decentralization is not enough unless the rules let many people act on their knowledge, bargain over gains, and contest harms.

> Progress requires both information and institutions: people must be able to discover opportunities, and the rules must let them pursue those opportunities without shifting unacceptable costs onto others.

::: {.discuss}
If a new technology would raise total income but harm a politically weak group, what kinds of rules would make the change more legitimate? What kinds would make it look like progress for some and extraction for others?
:::

```{=html}
<div class="quiz">
  <p class="quiz-q">How do the UOE chapters complicate a simple Hayekian market story?</p>
  <ol class="quiz-opts">
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="Hayek's account is about the knowledge problem, not a denial that institutions matter.">They show that prices contain no useful information.</li>
    <li data-correct="true" data-fb="Correct. UOE keeps the importance of decentralized action but asks who has the power and institutional permission to act.">They show that rules, outside options, and power shape who can use markets and on what terms.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="UOE does not reduce economics to government. It treats government, firms, households, and the environment as interacting parts of the economy.">They argue that government fully replaces markets.</li>
    <li data-correct="false" data-fb="UOE treats technology and incentives as important, but asks how gains and harms are distributed.">They argue that technology has no role in prosperity.</li>
  </ol>
</div>
```

::: {.instructor}
This is a good setup for Yuen Yuen Ang if you keep her in Session 11. Hayek gives a clean coordination argument; UOE gives students a more tractable model of rules and power; Ang complicates both by asking how development can begin under messy, transitional, and partially corrupt institutions.
:::

## Connections

**Builds on:** [Session 8](session08-silicon-valley-agglomeration.html) showed how regional institutions shape innovation. Session 10 scales up to the level of social rules: prices, property rights, outside options, and political decisions determine whether people can coordinate and challenge incumbents.

**Sets up:** Session 11 on escaping poverty traps will ask how poor societies build developmental capacity when the ideal institutions described here are incomplete, contested, or still emerging.

::: {.instructor}
**Arc note:** This session gives students the institutional baseline before the course turns to poverty traps and [**inequality**]{.term data-example="Rules, bargaining power, and outside options can protect opportunities for insiders while leaving outsiders with weaker choices and fewer ways to challenge harms."}. If they leave with only "markets good" or "institutions good," the session has failed. The target understanding is subtler: decentralized progress needs price signals, secure rights, and political institutions broad enough to let many people act.
:::

```{=html}
  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt

  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt
    question="Why do property rights matter for investment and innovation?"
    answer="People are more willing to invest, trade, and experiment when they expect contracts to be enforced and when they can keep enough of the returns from successful action. Property rights also define who can act and whose claims are protected.">
  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt
    question="What are institutions in the UOE 'rules of the game' sense?"
    answer="Institutions are the rules that structure an interaction: who can move, what actions are allowed, what each person can get if the interaction fails, and how conflicts are resolved.">
  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt
    question="What is an outside option?"
    answer="An outside option is what someone can get if they do not participate in a particular interaction. It matters because it shapes what they can demand in a bargain.">
  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt
    question="How does bargaining power affect the gains from cooperation?"
    answer="The side with stronger outside options, first-mover advantages, or institutional backing can often claim more of the gains from cooperation.">
  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt
    question="How do Hayek and UOE fit together?"
    answer="Hayek explains why decentralized knowledge and prices are necessary for coordination. UOE explains why rules, outside options, and power determine who can act on opportunities and how gains are divided.">
  </orbit-prompt>

  <orbit-prompt
    question="Give an example of a rule change that can alter economic power."
    answer="Examples include overtime law, environmental regulation, union protections, contract enforcement, zoning, immigration rules, or competition policy. Each changes what people can do and what they can get if bargaining fails.">
  </orbit-prompt>

</orbit-reviewarea>
```

## Reading guide

### Required

**Hayek, F. A.** "The Use of Knowledge in Society." *American Economic Review* 35, no. 4 (1945): 519-530. Free at [Econlib](https://www.econlib.org/library/Essays/hykKnw.html).

> **What to look for:** Do not read Hayek as a generic defense of markets. Read him as making a knowledge argument. What kinds of information are hard to centralize? How do prices help people respond to facts they do not personally know?
>
> **Key argument:** Prices are a coordination mechanism for dispersed knowledge; they allow millions of people to adjust to changing conditions without anyone needing to know the whole economy.
>
> **Bring to class:** One example where a price communicates useful information, and one example where price signals are incomplete or misleading.

**Halliday, Simon D., Luz Marina Arias, and Eric Bottorff.** *Understanding Our Economy 101*, Chapters 1 and 2 selections. CORE Econ, 2026. [Chapter 1](https://books.core-econ.org/understanding-our-economy/uoe-101/01-01.html) and [Chapter 2](https://books.core-econ.org/understanding-our-economy/uoe-101/02-01.html).

> **What to look for:** Focus on the mechanisms: rules of the game, outside options, bargaining power, cooperation, conflict, and democratic rule changes. Ask how a change in rules changes who can act and who captures the gains.
>
> **Key argument:** Economic interactions produce gains from cooperation, but the distribution of those gains depends on institutions: rules, outside options, power, and the ability to change the rules.
>
> **Bring to class:** One example of a rule change that would improve someone's outside option, and one example of a case where the price system alone would not resolve the conflict.

### Recommended

**North, Douglass C.** *Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance.* Cambridge University Press, 1990. Chapter 1.

> The canonical institutional-economics version of the argument: institutions are the humanly devised constraints that structure incentives, enforcement, and economic performance.

**Durlauf, Steven N.** "How the World Became Rich by Mark Koyama and Jared Rubin and *Slouching Towards Utopia* by J. Bradford DeLong: A Review Essay." *Journal of Economic Literature* 63, no. 1 (2025): 288-305, especially pp. 293-295.

> A useful bridge from Hayek to DeLong's Hayek/Polanyi frame, asking whether markets, liberty, distribution, and social justice can really be separated.

::: {.instructor}
**Teaching note on readings:** Hayek is short but dense; UOE gives the class a shared model they can work with. Pair them by asking students to distinguish four things: knowledge, incentives, outside options, and power. Prices help with knowledge; property rights help with incentives; institutions shape outside options and power.
:::
